Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: Kiet's eyes still scanned the streets with a mix of habit and instinct, his photographer's gaze now forever intertwined with the hypervigilance that had kept him alive in combat. It was a year ago that he'd returned from deployment, but the memories of those months in the war zone remained more real than any other moment in his life. He could still recall the sound of gunfire, the smell of smoke and sweat, and the weight of his rifle in his hands. It started with small things – jumpiness at car backfires or screams of children playing – but soon Kiet found himself constantly on edge, unable to relax even when he was alone in his apartment. He'd try to focus on editing photos for hours, only to find his mind drifting back to the worst moments: the ambush that killed two of his squad members, the sounds of their cries still echoing in his ears. Taking risks had become a way for Kiet to feel something other than numbness and guilt. He'd drive recklessly, pushing speeds on deserted roads, or take unnecessary risks while shooting in abandoned buildings. It was as if he needed to test his own mortality, to prove that he was still alive. His friends and family worried about him, but Kiet couldn't explain why he felt drawn to danger – only that it made the memories recede for a little while. When memories did surface, they brought with them a tide of rage. He'd be in the middle of a shoot, camera in hand, when suddenly he'd see his squad leader's face, remember the sound of gunfire, and feel an overwhelming urge to smash everything around him. It was as if the past had reached out and grabbed him by the throat, leaving him gasping for air. Kiet tried to avoid triggers – loud noises, crowded places – but they seemed to lurk everywhere. He'd be walking through a market when a vendor's shout would send him spinning back into the chaos of combat. The memories were so vivid that he sometimes felt like he was reliving them all over again, his heart racing and palms slick with sweat. In quieter moments, Kiet couldn't shake the feeling that he didn't belong anywhere anymore. He'd grown up in a tight-knit Vietnamese-American community, but now even familiar faces seemed foreign to him. People's smiles and laughter grated on his nerves; he was certain they couldn't understand what he'd been through. He mistrusted everyone – friends, family, even himself. Kiet felt like he should have protected his squad members that day, that somehow it was all his fault. He replayed the events in his head, wondering if there was something – anything – he could have done differently. The weight of those 'what ifs' crushed him at times, leaving him feeling like a failure. Photography had been Kiet's passion before deployment, but now even that felt tainted by his experiences. He couldn't bear to take portraits of happy families or smiling children; it all seemed so superficial compared to the reality he'd witnessed. His camera gathered dust as Kiet struggled to find meaning in anything he did. It was a particularly brutal memory – one that had been triggered by a chance encounter with an old comrade – that finally made Kiet realize he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this, constantly looking over his shoulder, waiting for the next flashback or nightmare. As he sat in his darkened apartment, surrounded by the detritus of his own broken dreams, Kiet knew it was time to face whatever demons had taken up residence inside him. With a sense of trepidation and hope, Kiet picked up the phone and dialed the number for a local VA support group. For the first time in months, he allowed himself to imagine that maybe – just maybe – there was a way out of this darkness, and back into the light.
